title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
summary: Nearly two centuries of British colonial rule left India in 1947 with a stagnant, backward agriculture, a weak and narrow industrial base, a foreign trade geared to British interests and very poor health and literacy indicators. This chapter examines the state of agriculture, industry, foreign trade, demography, occupational structure and infrastructure at independence, and the few positive legacies of colonial rule.

notes.heading: Low level of economic development under colonial rule
notes.html:
Before British rule India had an independent economy with flourishing agriculture and handicrafts (cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone work) famous worldwide. The colonial government's main aim was to make India a supplier of raw materials for British industry and a market for British manufactured goods, not to develop the Indian economy.

  • National and per capita income were low. Estimates by economists such as Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai showed this; V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates for the colonial period are regarded as the most significant.
  • Studies indicate that in the first half of the 20th century real output grew at less than 2% a year and per capita output at only about 0.5% a year.
  • The British made no serious attempt to estimate national income for policy purposes; the estimates that existed were by individuals and were not fully consistent.

notes.heading: Agricultural sector: stagnation and deterioration
notes.html:
India was mainly agrarian: more than 85% of the population lived in villages and depended directly or indirectly on agriculture. Yet agriculture was stagnant, with low productivity, despite some growth in the area under cultivation.

Causes of stagnation

  • Land revenue systems: under the zamindari system (Permanent Settlement in Bengal Presidency), profits went to zamindars rather than cultivators. Zamindars collected maximum rent without investing in land improvement. Fixed dates for revenue payment, failing which rights were lost, made conditions harsh.
  • Commercialisation of agriculture: farmers were pushed to grow cash crops such as indigo, jute and cotton for British industry. It increased yields of cash crops in some areas but did not raise farmers' welfare, and food grain production suffered.
  • Low level of technology, little use of fertilisers, inadequate irrigation facilities and frequent famines.
  • Indebtedness of farmers and fragmentation of holdings.

At partition, much of the well-irrigated land of undivided Punjab and Sindh went to West Pakistan, and the jute-growing areas of Bengal went to East Pakistan, while the jute mills remained in India. This added to India's food and raw material problem.

notes.heading: Industrial sector: de-industrialisation and a weak base
notes.html:
India could not develop a sound industrial base under colonial rule. The decline of India's world-famous handicraft industries was not accompanied by the growth of modern industry.

Twin motives behind de-industrialisation

  1. To reduce India to an exporter of raw materials for Britain's modern industries.
  2. To turn India into a large market for the finished products of those industries.

Features of the industrial sector

  • Modern industry began in the second half of the 19th century but grew very slowly. Cotton textile mills were mainly Indian-owned and concentrated in western India (Maharashtra, Gujarat); jute mills were mainly foreign-owned and concentrated in Bengal.
  • Iron and steel began in the early 20th century; the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was set up in 1907. A few industries such as sugar, cement and paper came up after the Second World War.
  • No capital goods industry worth the name existed to produce machine tools for further industrialisation.
  • The growth rate of the new industrial sector and its share in GDP remained very small.
  • The public sector was limited to railways, power, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

notes.heading: Foreign trade
notes.html:
India was an important trading nation from ancient times, but colonial policies changed the structure, composition and volume of its trade.

  • Composition: India became an exporter of primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute, and an importer of finished consumer goods (cotton, silk and woollen clothes) and capital goods such as light machinery from British factories.
  • Direction: Britain kept a monopoly over India's trade; more than half of India's foreign trade was with Britain, and the rest with a few countries such as China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Persia (Iran).
  • The opening of the Suez Canal (1869) cut the cost and time of shipping between Britain and India and further intensified British control.
  • Export surplus without benefit: India had a large export surplus, but it did not bring gold or silver into the country. It was used to pay for the expenses of the British administration in India, its wars and the import of invisible items (shipping, insurance, banking). This is often called the drain of Indian wealth.
  • Shortage of essential goods such as food grains, clothes and kerosene in the domestic market resulted.

notes.heading: Demographic condition
notes.html:
The first official census of British India was conducted in 1881. Detailed population data was collected through regular censuses thereafter.

  • Before 1921 India was in the first stage of demographic transition, with both birth and death rates high, so population grew slowly. 1921 is called the year of the great divide, after which the second stage began: death rates fell while birth rates remained high, so population grew faster.
  • Social indicators were very poor: overall literacy was less than 16%, and female literacy was only about 7%.
  • Public health facilities were inadequate; water- and air-borne diseases were widespread and caused many deaths.
  • The overall mortality rate was very high; the infant mortality rate was about 218 per thousand (compared with a figure below 30 per thousand in recent years).
  • Life expectancy was only about 32 years.
  • Extensive poverty existed due to lack of income and employment opportunities.

notes.heading: Occupational structure
notes.html:
Occupational structure refers to the distribution of the workforce among different sectors.

SectorApproximate share of workforce at independence
Agriculture (primary)70–75%
Manufacturing (secondary)about 10%
Services (tertiary)15–20%
  • The structure remained almost unchanged during colonial rule, showing a lack of structural change.
  • Regional variation: parts of the then Madras Presidency, Bombay and Bengal saw a fall in dependence on agriculture and a rise in manufacturing and services, while in states such as Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab the share of agriculture actually rose.

notes.heading: Infrastructure and its real motive
notes.html:
The British developed railways, roads, ports, water transport and posts and telegraphs. However, the aim was not to provide basic amenities to Indians but to serve colonial interests: administration, movement of the army to maintain control, and transport of raw materials from the interior to ports for export.

  • Railways were introduced in the mid-19th century (the first passenger train ran between Bombay and Thane in 1853). Positive effects: people could travel long distances, geographical and cultural barriers were broken, and commercialisation of agriculture was encouraged. Negative effects: commercialisation weakened the self-sufficiency of village economies; the volume of exports grew but the benefits seldom went to Indians.
  • Roads built were mostly for military and trade purposes; there was little all-weather rural road access.
  • Inland waterways were often uneconomical, e.g. the Coast Canal on the Orissa coast was built at great cost but could not compete with the railways.
  • Posts and electric telegraph served the purpose of maintaining law and order.

notes.heading: Positive legacies and the challenge at independence
notes.html:
Some aspects of colonial rule had positive side effects:

  • Introduction of railways, which helped unify the national market and broke regional isolation.
  • Development of ports, posts and telegraphs, and a beginning of modern industry.
  • Commercialisation of agriculture, which introduced market orientation.
  • A unified administrative system and the beginnings of modern banking and education.

Challenges facing independent India: reviving stagnant agriculture, building a strong industrial base including capital goods, reducing poverty and unemployment, expanding health and education, and creating infrastructure for development. These challenges shaped the five-year plans that followed.

keyTerms.definition: Control by a foreign power over a territory, its people and resources, mainly for the economic benefit of the ruling country.
A land revenue system in which zamindars collected rent from cultivators and paid a fixed revenue to the government, keeping the rest; introduced through the Permanent Settlement in Bengal.
Production of crops for sale in the market rather than for self-consumption; under British rule, a forced shift to cash crops like indigo and jute.
The decline of India's traditional handicraft industries under colonial rule without the replacement by modern industries.
Industries that produce machines and tools used to produce other goods; almost absent in colonial India.
The transfer of India's resources, including its export surplus, to Britain to pay for administration, wars and invisible services.
The change in population growth over time as birth and death rates move from high to low levels.
1921, after which India moved to the second stage of demographic transition, with population rising steadily.
The number of infants dying before reaching one year of age per thousand live births.
The distribution of the working population among different occupations or sectors of the economy.
Excess of the value of exports over the value of imports.

mcqs.q: Which economist's estimates of national income during the colonial period are considered the most significant?
options: Dadabhai Naoroji
William Digby
V.K.R.V. Rao
Findlay Shirras
mcqs.explanation: Several individuals estimated India's income, but V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates are regarded as the most significant for the colonial period.

mcqs.q: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in:
mcqs.explanation: TISCO was set up in 1907, marking the start of the iron and steel industry. 1853 relates to the first passenger train and 1921 to the great divide in demography.

mcqs.q: Which year is called the 'year of the great divide' in India's demographic history?
mcqs.explanation: After 1921 the death rate began to fall steadily while the birth rate stayed high, moving India into the second stage of demographic transition.

mcqs.q: Under colonial rule, India mainly exported:
options: Primary products such as raw cotton, jute and indigo
Heavy machinery
Finished woollen clothes
Capital goods
mcqs.explanation: Colonial policy turned India into a supplier of raw materials for British industry and an importer of finished goods.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): India's export surplus during colonial rule did not lead to an inflow of gold or silver into India.
Reason (R): The surplus was used to meet the expenses of the British government in India, its wars and the import of invisible services.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: The surplus was absorbed by administrative and war expenses and payments for shipping, banking and insurance, so it did not increase India's wealth. R explains A.

mcqs.q: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 led to:
options: A decline in British trade with India
Diversion of Indian trade towards the USA
Intensified British control over India's foreign trade
The end of the zamindari system
mcqs.explanation: The canal cut the cost and time of transport between Britain and India, strengthening Britain's hold over India's trade.

mcqs.q: At the time of independence the share of the workforce in agriculture was approximately:
mcqs.explanation: About 70–75% of the workforce depended on agriculture, with around 10% in manufacturing and 15–20% in services.

mcqs.q:
Read the statements:
Statement 1: The jute mills in colonial India were mostly owned by Indians and located in western India.
Statement 2: Cotton textile mills were mostly Indian-owned and located in western India.
options: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
mcqs.explanation: Jute mills were mainly foreign-owned and concentrated in Bengal; cotton mills were largely Indian-owned and located in Maharashtra and Gujarat.

mcqs.q: The main purpose of building railways in colonial India was to:
options: Provide cheap travel to Indian villagers
Promote Indian handicrafts
Develop the capital goods industry
Serve colonial interests such as moving raw materials to ports and troops across the country
mcqs.explanation: Railways were built mainly for administrative and military control and to carry raw materials to ports and British goods inland.

mcqs.q: Which of the following was a cause of stagnation in agriculture during British rule?
options: Heavy investment in irrigation by zamindars
Use of high yielding variety seeds
The zamindari system, under which zamindars extracted rent without improving land
Land ceiling laws
mcqs.explanation: Zamindars were interested only in collecting rent and did little to improve agriculture. HYV seeds and land ceilings came after independence.

mcqs.q: At independence, the literacy rate of India was:
options: Less than 16%
About 30%
About 45%
About 52%
mcqs.explanation: Overall literacy was below 16%, and female literacy was only about 7%.

mcqs.q: Partition affected the Indian jute industry because:
options: All jute mills went to Pakistan
Most jute-growing areas went to East Pakistan while the mills remained in India
Britain banned jute exports
Jute was replaced by synthetic fibres
mcqs.explanation: Raw jute was mainly grown in East Bengal (East Pakistan), while the mills were around Calcutta in India, so the industry lost its raw material base.

questions.q: What was the main focus of the economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India?
questions.answerHtml: To protect and promote the economic interests of Britain, by turning India into a supplier of raw materials for British industries and a market for British manufactured goods.

questions.q: Name any two notable estimators of India's per capita income during the colonial period.
questions.answerHtml: Dadabhai Naoroji and V.K.R.V. Rao (others: William Digby, Findlay Shirras, R.C. Desai).

questions.q: What was the twofold motive behind the systematic de-industrialisation of India by the colonial government?
questions.answerHtml:
1. To reduce India to a mere exporter of important raw materials (cotton, jute, indigo) for the upcoming modern industries in Britain.
  2. To turn India into a vast market for the finished products of those British industries, so that their expansion could continue to benefit Britain.

As a result, India's world-famous handicrafts declined, artisans lost their livelihood, and no modern industry developed in their place.

questions.q: Discuss the demographic condition of India on the eve of independence.
questions.answerHtml:
• Before 1921 India was in the first stage of demographic transition; after 1921 (the year of the great divide) it entered the second stage with a falling death rate and high birth rate.
  • Overall literacy was below 16% and female literacy around 7%.
  • Public health facilities were poor; water- and air-borne diseases were widespread. Infant mortality was very high (about 218 per thousand) and life expectancy only about 32 years.
  • Lack of income and employment led to extensive poverty.

questions.q: 'Indian agriculture was stagnant during British rule.' Give any four reasons.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Land settlement system: under the zamindari system, the zamindars collected as much rent as possible from cultivators and made no investment in improving land. Profits went to them, not to the tillers.
  2. Harsh revenue terms: revenue had to be paid on fixed dates regardless of the harvest, failing which rights over land were lost; this left cultivators impoverished.
  3. Forced commercialisation: farmers were made to grow cash crops such as indigo for British industry, reducing food grain production without improving their incomes.
  4. Low technology and inputs: lack of irrigation, negligible use of fertilisers and improved seeds, and indebtedness of farmers kept productivity very low.

questions.q: 'Railways had both positive and negative effects on the Indian economy during colonial rule.' Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Positive effects:

  • People could travel long distances cheaply, which broke geographical and cultural barriers and helped national integration.
  • Railways encouraged the commercialisation of agriculture by linking villages to wider markets.

Negative effects:

  • Commercialisation weakened the self-sufficiency of village economies; farmers became dependent on distant markets.
  • Railways mainly helped carry raw materials to ports for export and British goods inland, so the volume of exports rose but the benefits seldom reached Indians.
  • They also eased the flow of cheap British goods that hurt Indian handicrafts.

questions.q: Describe the state of India's foreign trade during the colonial period.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Composition changed: India became an exporter of primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute, and an importer of finished consumer goods (cotton, silk and woollen clothes) and capital goods such as light machinery from Britain.
  2. British monopoly: Britain controlled India's exports and imports; more than half of India's trade was with Britain, and the remainder with a few countries like China, Ceylon and Persia.
  3. Suez Canal: its opening in 1869 made shipping cheaper and faster, which strengthened British control over Indian trade.
  4. Export surplus but no gain: India generated a large export surplus, but it was used to pay for the expenses of the British administration, its wars and the import of invisible services like shipping and banking. This led to a drain of wealth rather than an accumulation of gold and silver.
  5. Domestic shortages: since trade served British needs, essential goods such as food grains, clothing and kerosene were scarce in the domestic market.

Thus foreign trade under colonial rule served British interests and contributed little to India's development.

questions.q: Describe the condition of the industrial sector of India on the eve of independence.
questions.answerHtml:
• Decline of handicrafts: India's world-famous handicraft industries collapsed due to discriminatory tariffs and competition from cheap machine-made British goods. This led to unemployment of artisans and a fall in demand for local goods.
  • Slow growth of modern industry: modern industries began in the second half of the 19th century. Cotton textile mills (largely Indian-owned) came up in western India and jute mills (largely foreign-owned) in Bengal. The iron and steel industry began with TISCO in 1907. Sugar, cement and paper industries came up after the Second World War.
  • Absence of capital goods industries: there were hardly any industries producing machine tools, so further industrialisation depended on imports.
  • Low growth and small share: the growth rate of the industrial sector was very low and its contribution to GDP small.
  • Limited public sector: the public sector was confined to railways, power generation, communications, ports and a few departmental undertakings.

India therefore inherited a weak and lopsided industrial base, which made rapid industrialisation a central goal of planning after independence.
